tasks.locator: Abstract; Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note; Study selection, abstraction, and analysis; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
tasks.extracted: The 2024 review by route: a systematic review without meta-analysis, guided by PRISMA, with no protocol or registration stated. Search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; peer-reviewed English-language articles from January 2009 to December 2023 reporting the route of administration, with cannabis confirmed by drug screening; studies including other illicit drugs, or people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions, excluded. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco. 1,873 records, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis of tweets, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Abstract selection was independent (kappa 0.89). The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grades and no appraisal of individual studies are reported, and nothing was pooled.

tasks.locator: Results › Empirical studies › Respiratory effects, 1st and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Kempker 2015, Tan 2009, Hancox 2010, Tashkin 2012, Fiorelli 2013 rows)
tasks.extracted: Smoking and breathing, single studies as the review relays them: NHANES 2007 to 2010 (Kempker 2015; US adults, cross-sectional): cough, cold, phlegm or respiratory illness in the past 7 days in 16.9%, 22.4%, 26.1% and 24.0% of people who smoked cannabis on 0, 1–5, 6–20 and more than 20 of the past 30 days, and wheeze in the past year in 12.4%, 19.8%, 23.3% and 26.5% (as printed, unadjusted); more than 20 joint-years against no exposure, FEV1/FVC below 70% OR 2.1 (95% CI 1.1 to 3.9), with no association at lower cumulative exposure. Vancouver (Tan 2009; random sample of 878 people aged 40 or more, spirometry): people who had smoked at least 50 cannabis cigarettes and no tobacco were not at significantly greater risk of COPD or respiratory symptoms; people who had smoked both had higher odds of COPD (OR 2.90, 1.53 to 5.51) and of symptoms (OR 2.39, 1.58 to 3.62), adjusted for age, asthma and comorbidities; the review does not name the comparison group, and its text calls this smoking cannabis in a joint combined with tobacco while its Table 4 describes people who smoked both. Dunedin (Hancox 2010; 1,037 people followed to age 32): cumulative use associated with higher FVC, lung volumes and airway resistance but not with FEV1, the FEV1/FVC ratio or gas transfer. Los Angeles (Tashkin 2012; 299 people followed 9.8 years): more chronic bronchitis at follow-up with continued cannabis smoking than in never or former smokers. Naples (Fiorelli 2013; people treated for spontaneous pneumothorax, 13 who smoked cannabis and 140 who did not, 135 of them tobacco smokers): bullae in 8 (62%) against 110 (78%) overall and, under age 35, in 7 of 10 against 3 of 10, though the text says cannabis smoking predisposed to bullous lung disease.

tasks.locator: Results › Empirical studies › Cardiovascular effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Respiratory effects, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Table 4 (Cooper and Haney 2009, Newmeyer 2017 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning Second
tasks.extracted: Routes compared in the same people (laboratory studies, second-hand): Newmeyer 2017 (double-blind, placebo-controlled, double-dummy crossover; 11 adults who smoked cannabis frequently and 9 occasionally; smoked, vaporised and oral cannabis in separate sessions): smoking produced significantly greater increases in expired carbon monoxide than vaporisation from 0.25 to 6 h after dosing; route had no significant effect on breathing rate or blood pressure; heart rate rose above placebo by 12.2 (smoked) and 10.7 (vaporised) beats a minute at 0.5 h and by 13.0 and 10.2 at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, increases that did not differ significantly between routes. Cooper and Haney 2009 (24 healthy volunteers; blunts against joints of the same cannabis at three strengths including inactive): more expired carbon monoxide after blunts at every strength (p ≤ 0.01); joints gave greater increases in plasma THC; heart-rate increases were equivalent. The review's Discussion gives the Newmeyer sample as n = 11, against 11 and 9 in its Table 4.

tasks.locator: Results › Literature reviews, 3rd paragraph; Table 3 (Russell 2017 row); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Respiratory effects, 2nd paragraph; Table 4 (Newmeyer 2017, Shiplo 2016, Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 rows); Discussion, paragraph beginning Nevertheless
tasks.extracted: Vaping in the review (second-hand): three empirical studies have a vaping arm, and all compare vaping with smoking, not with no use. Newmeyer 2017 (the laboratory crossover; dried cannabis in a vaporizer). Shiplo 2016 (online survey of 364 adults approved to use medical cannabis in Canada, April to June 2015): a vaporizer and eating in food were rated lower in perceived harm (cough, phlegm, chest tightness) than smoking, and the number of side effects lower for the vaporizer than for smoking or eating. Van Dam and Earleywine 2010 (pre/post design, no control group): 22 people who used cannabis frequently, were not interested in treatment and reported at least two respiratory symptoms used a vaporizer for 1 month; the 12 who did not develop a respiratory illness during the trial had fewer symptoms (t(11) = 6.22) and higher FVC (t(11) = 2.90, p = 0.007 as printed), while FEV1 did not change significantly (p = 0.053 as printed); the amount used a day fell slightly and not significantly (p = 0.10 as printed), though the text says vaping reduced it. The scoping review of Russell 2017 is reported as finding that vaping reduced respiratory symptoms. The text's list of vaping studies also names Kaczor 2021 and Pepin 2023, which Table 4 gives as edible studies in children. No included study examined THC oil cartridges, followed people who vape over time, or compared them with people who do not use cannabis; the authors call for research on long-term outcomes of vaping and on vaping-associated lung injury with THC-containing e-liquids. Editors' calculation: two-tailed p values for t(11) = 2.90 and 1.77 and t(18) = 1.34 are about 0.014, 0.10 and 0.20, so the printed values match one-tailed tests, and the printed d values equal 2t divided by the square root of the degrees of freedom, a formula for two independent groups.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraphs beginning Nevertheless, First, Second and Third; Strength and limitations; Conclusion; Disclosure statement; Funding
tasks.extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled or appraised (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).

tasks.locator: Abstract (Methods, Results); Materials and methods › Swedish male conscripts' files; Measurement of cannabis use
tasks.extracted: Cohort and exposure: 49,321 men aged 18 to 20 conscripted for compulsory Swedish military service in 1969–1970 (more than 97% of Swedish men of that age; 2–3% were excused for disqualifying conditions), linked to the Patient Register, the National Cause-of-Death Register and the Total Population Register. Cannabis use was self-reported once, at conscription, in a non-anonymous questionnaire: ever against never, and lifetime frequency (never, once, 2–4, 5–10, 11–50 and more than 50 times); this paper calls more than 50 times heavy use. At baseline 10.5% (5,156) reported lifetime use and 1.7% (831) more than 50 uses.

tasks.locator: Materials and methods › Measurement of tobacco use; Potential confounders; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1 (never and more-than-50 columns)
tasks.extracted: Tobacco and other covariates: tobacco was measured once, at conscription, as cigarettes smoked a day (none 41.4%, 1–5 a day 11.2%, 6–10 20.7%, 11–20 23.1%, more than 20 3.6%), collapsed into three bands for the models: none, 1–10 and more than 10 a day. Of the 831 men reporting more than 50 cannabis uses, 60 (7.2%) did not smoke tobacco, 242 (29.1%) smoked 1–10 a day, 514 (61.8%) more than 10 and 15 (1.8%) gave no tobacco answer; of the 40,397 men reporting never using cannabis, 18,100 (44.8%) did not smoke tobacco, 12,725 (31.5%) smoked 1–10 a day and 9,364 (23.2%) more than 10. Alcohol above 250 g a week: 23.1% against 2.3%. Respiratory conditions diagnosed at conscription (chronic bronchitis, emphysema, pneumonia or asthma) about 2% in each group; socioeconomic status from occupation in the 1970 census. The Results say about 91% of the heaviest band reported some tobacco use.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4 (more than 50 times row; footnotes a and b)
tasks.extracted: More than 50 lifetime uses at conscription against never, Cox regression on 44,257 men with 179 lung cancers: hazard ratio 3.72 (95% CI 1.96 to 7.06) crude, 2.24 (1.17 to 4.29) adjusted for tobacco in three bands, and 2.12 (1.08 to 4.14) fully adjusted for tobacco, alcohol (four levels), respiratory conditions at conscription and socioeconomic status in 1970. The authors describe it as more than a twofold risk even after these adjustments.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd to 4th paragraphs; Table 3; Table 4 (once to 11–50 times rows); Table 2
tasks.extracted: No association for any use once tobacco was counted, and no gradient below the heaviest band: ever against never, crude 1.90 (1.30 to 2.75), tobacco-adjusted 1.25 (0.85 to 1.83), fully adjusted 1.25 (0.84 to 1.87), on 44,285 men with 179 cancers, the authors saying tobacco adjustment greatly attenuated the risk. Lifetime frequency, fully adjusted against never: once 1.52 (0.77 to 3.01), 2–4 times 0.66 (0.27 to 1.62), 5–10 times 0.68 (0.21 to 2.16), 11–50 times 1.68 (0.77 to 3.66); crude, once 2.07 (1.06 to 4.06) and 11–50 times 2.69 (1.26 to 5.74). The authors state that the results did not show a clear dose–response relationship. Tobacco in the same models showed a strong gradient: fully adjusted 2.34 (1.47 to 3.70) for 1–10 and 5.03 (3.23 to 7.81) for more than 10 cigarettes a day against none.

tasks.locator: Materials and methods › Study outcome; Validity of lung cancer outcome codes; Statistical analyses; Results, 1st paragraph; Fig. 1 legend; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Follow-up and outcome: from 1 January 1970 (1 October 1969 for two men) to lung cancer, death from other causes, emigration or 31 December 2009, about 1.9 million person-years in each analysis. Lung cancer (ICD-8/9 162; ICD-10 C33–C34) came from the Patient Register (inpatient care, any diagnostic position) to the end of 2009 and from the Cause-of-Death Register (underlying cause) to the end of 2006; the authors cite 78% to 99% concordance between registers. 189 men had incident lung cancer (95 in both registers, 88 in the Patient Register only, 6 in the death register only), 2,958 (6.0%) died of other causes and 930 (1.9%) emigrated; ten cancers were excluded for missing predictors. Cancers by cannabis group are shown only in Figure 1, a stacked bar chart by year (values not extracted), so no absolute risk by group can be given. The authors note that the only earlier cohort ended at a mean age of 42 and that the median age at a first lung cancer diagnosis is about 70. Editors' calculation: men born in 1949 to 1951 were 58 to 60 at the end of follow-up, and 189 of 49,321 (0.38%, about 4 in 1,000) had a lung cancer record by then.

tasks.locator: Materials and methods › Missing data; Results, 5th paragraph and its continuation after Table 4
tasks.extracted: Missing answers: cannabis answers were missing for 3,768 men (7.64%; ever use) and 3,800 (7.70%; frequency). Against men reporting never using cannabis, these men were not more likely to develop lung cancer: ever-use item crude 0.52 (0.24 to 1.10), tobacco-adjusted 0.47 (0.21 to 1.07), fully adjusted 0.41 (0.17 to 0.99); frequency item 0.51 (0.24 to 1.09), 0.47 (0.21 to 1.06) and 0.40 (0.16 to 0.98). The authors ran these models to check whether the men who did not answer had used cannabis heavily; the paper does not explain their lower risk.

tasks.locator: Results, last paragraph (Supplemental Tables 1–2); Discussion, 3rd, 5th and 6th paragraphs; Conclusions
tasks.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: no detailed information on cannabis or tobacco use before conscription and none after it; residual confounding by tobacco possible, since more than 91% of the heavy group reported some tobacco smoking at conscription; participants may have mixed tobacco into cannabis cigarettes, which would inflate the cannabis-related risk, and whether this was common in Sweden in 1969–1970 is unclear; non-anonymous reports may have led to under-reporting of cannabis use, while anecdotal information suggests some men inflated their use to be exempted from military training. Analyses stratified by tobacco (Supplemental Tables 1 and 2, not available to this reader) gave unstable or inestimable results, because most people who used cannabis, especially frequently, also used tobacco and lung cancer was uncommon. The authors argue that changes in use after conscription would bias the estimates toward the null. Their conclusion calls the finding initial longitudinal evidence, requiring further replication, that cannabis use might raise lung cancer risk, and the Discussion proposes its use in drug-prevention programmes. Editors' note: later tobacco smoking, if more common in the men who used cannabis, would bias the estimate away from the null; the paper covers this only as residual confounding by tobacco.

tasks.locator: Methods, 1st, 2nd, 4th and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Products, not people: dispensaries in San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle were picked at random from an Internet directory until three per city were found that sold at least one edible in each of three categories (baked goods, beverages, candy or chocolate) with a specific delta-9-THC content on the label. Between August and October 2014, purchasers with a physician's letter and no history of buying edibles bought as wide a variety as possible within $400 per city; purchasers, but not dispensary staff, knew the products would be tested. Whole packages were homogenized and two samples tested by high-performance liquid chromatography, averaged and scaled to the product's weight; where the two differed by more than 10% (37 products) the whole product was analysed. Within 10% of the label counted as accurate, more than 10% above as underlabelled and more than 10% below as overlabelled.

tasks.locator: Results, 1st paragraph, 1st sentence (p. 2491); Table 1, Overall (3 Cities) rows (p. 2492)
tasks.extracted: Of 75 products (47 brands), THC was within 10% of the label in 13 (17%), more than 10% above it in 17 (23%) and more than 10% below it in 45 (60%). Mean deviation (SD): within, -3% (4), largest 9%; above, +28% (13), largest +55% (measured 34 to 1,236 mg against labelled 20 to 1,000 mg); below, -47% (29), largest -99% (measured under 1 to 267 mg against labelled 2 to 325 mg). By type (within / above / below): baked goods 2 / 7 / 13; beverages 3 / 2 / 8; candy or chocolate 8 / 8 / 24. Editors' calculation: 62 of 75 (82.7%) outside 10%; Wilson 95% intervals 10.4% to 27.4% (within), 14.7% to 33.3% (above) and 48.7% to 70.3% (below); the city rows (-44%, -55% and -61% for 20, 7 and 18 products) give an n-weighted mean shortfall of -52.5%, not the overall row's -47%.

tasks.locator: Table 1, San Francisco, Los Angeles and Seattle rows
tasks.extracted: Within 10% / more than 10% above / more than 10% below the THC label: San Francisco 8 (25%) / 4 (13%) / 20 (62%) of 32 products; Los Angeles 4 (20%) / 9 (45%) / 7 (35%) of 20; Seattle 1 (4%) / 4 (17%) / 18 (78%) of 23. Mean shortfall of the products below their label: San Francisco -44%, Los Angeles -55%, Seattle -61%; largest -93%, -99% and -99%.

tasks.locator: JAMA 2015;314(2):188, Correction, 'Incorrect Labels in Text and in Table 1 Column Headings', right column
tasks.extracted: The correction gives the Results as: 17% accurately labelled, 23% underlabelled and 60% overlabelled for THC; underlabelled products (more THC than the label) likeliest in Los Angeles and overlabelled products (less THC) in Seattle (chi-squared 12.94, P = .01); for CBD, 4 products underlabelled and 9 overlabelled; the third column of Table 1 headed Underlabelled and the fourth Overlabelled. The saved PDF of the letter (p. 2491) prints the city sentence and the CBD sentence the other way round, against its own Table 1; the correction is followed.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd paragraph, 3rd sentence as corrected in JAMA 2015;314(2):188 (p. 2491); Table 2 (p. 2493)
tasks.extracted: 44 of 75 products (59%) had detectable CBD; only 13 printed a CBD content, of which, as corrected, 4 held more than 10% more and 9 more than 10% less than labelled. Median THC:CBD ratio of products with detectable CBD 36:1; 7 had ratios below 10:1 and 1 a 1:1 ratio. Measured content per product (measured product content), mg, median (interquartile range as printed) and range: THC 54 (99), under 1 to 1,236; THCA 2 (15), under 1 to 173; CBD 2 (3), under 1 to 51. So none of the 13 CBD labels was within 10% (editors' arithmetic).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: The authors write that the products, though unregulated, failed basic label-accuracy standards for pharmaceuticals; that more than half held significantly less cannabinoid than labelled (meaning beyond the 10% limit; no statistical test per product), some with negligible THC, and may not give the desired medical benefit; and that others held significantly more THC than labelled, which they say puts patients at risk of adverse effects, citing two sources (no effects were measured). They state that few cities, dispensaries and products were included and that, because no source lists all dispensaries and many products have no cannabinoid label, a true random sample was not possible and the results may not generalize.

tasks.locator: Author Affiliations (p. 2491); Author Contributions, Conflict of Interest Disclosures, Funding/Support, Role of the Funder/Sponsor (p. 2493)
tasks.extracted: Funded by Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine except the cost of analytical testing, which Werc Shop Laboratories covered; neither, the paper says, had a role in the design, conduct, data, manuscript or decision to submit. Four of the six authors are affiliated with Werc Shop Laboratory (Pasadena, California; Bellevue, Washington); concept and design are credited to Vandrey, J. Raber, Douglass and Bonn-Miller, and supervision to Vandrey, J. Raber and Douglass. Bonn-Miller reported personal fees and nonfinancial support from Tilray (Division of Privateer Holdings) and travel reimbursement from Americans for Safe Access; no other disclosures. The paper does not describe these organisations.

tasks.locator: Methods › Data Source, Case Selection Criteria, General Characteristics Data and Clinical Effects and Therapies (p. 2, continued on p. 3)
tasks.extracted: Retrospective analysis of aggregate National Poison Data System data (exposures reported to the 55 regional poison control centres serving the United States and its territories), queried for the generic code for edible cannabis in children younger than 6, 2017 to 2021 (2021 preliminary): 7,043 cases. 2,216 cases not followed to a known outcome were left out of the analysis of clinical effects and treatments, leaving 4,827. In 2019 the codes for decreased mental status were replaced by graded CNS depression, combined by the authors into one category. Chi-squared tests compared 2017 to 2019 with 2020 to 2021.

tasks.locator: Results › General Characteristics, 1st paragraph, and Figure 1 data labels, read on the rendered page (p. 3); Table 1, Number of cases per year (p. 4); Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 5)
tasks.extracted: Calls by year: 207 (2017), 590 (2018), 983 (2019), 2,209 (2020), 3,054 (2021); 7,043 in all, an increase the paper gives as 1375.0%. Per 1,000 calls about children under 6: 0.2 in 2017 and 3.6 in 2021 (0.02% and 0.36%; P < .05), with Figure 1 labels 0.6, 1.1 and 2.5 for 2018 to 2020. All calls about children aged 0 to 5 fell from 956,871 to 846,296 over the five years. Editors' arithmetic: 14.75 times (1375.4%) from 2017 to 2021.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (p. 5, continued on p. 6), 2nd and 4th paragraphs (p. 6), 9th paragraph, on limitations (p. 7)
tasks.extracted: The authors could not determine the number of cases per state and write that the increases are believed to be associated with more states allowing adult recreational use; they suggest COVID-related quarantines and school or daycare closures may have played a role; for the changes in disposition they write that it is unknown why they occurred, suggesting clinicians' comfort and experience, bed availability, more THC per package or more products bought, or more severe effects. Limitations: only exposures reported to US poison centres, so the numbers underestimate the actual number; it is unknown whether more reporting or less stigma contributed to the rise; the data depend on what callers report and on coding; missing data and loss to follow-up.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Methods › Search strategy; Table 1 and its note; Study selection, abstraction, and analysis; Results, 1st paragraph; Figure 1
tasks.extracted: The 2024 review by route: a systematic review without meta-analysis, guided by PRISMA, with no protocol or registration stated. Search of Web of Science, ProQuest, PsycINFO, Embase and Medline (the Abstract also names Scopus) in November–December 2019, updated August–December 2023, plus reference lists; peer-reviewed English-language articles from January 2009 to December 2023 reporting the route of administration, with cannabis confirmed by drug screening; studies including other illicit drugs, or people with pre-existing heart or lung conditions, excluded. In Table 1 the cannabis terms are combined with AND NOT Tobacco. 1,873 records, 110 full texts, 42 included: 6 case reports or series, 21 literature reviews and 15 empirical studies (2 randomised trials, 5 retrospective analyses, 1 content analysis of tweets, 3 longitudinal studies, 3 cross-sectional surveys, 1 pre/post study). Abstract selection was independent (kappa 0.89). The Methods say the strength of evidence was graded for each outcome, but no grades and no appraisal of individual studies are reported, and nothing was pooled.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Results); Results › Empirical studies, 1st paragraph; Cardiovascular effects, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 4 (Cao 2016, Kaczor 2021, Newmeyer 2017, Pepin 2023, Shiplo 2016 rows); Discussion, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Oral route in the review (second-hand): five empirical studies have an oral arm. In adults, the Newmeyer 2017 laboratory crossover found heart rate 13.0 and 10.2 beats a minute above placebo at 1.5 and 3 h after oral cannabis, not significantly different from smoked or vaporised cannabis, and no effect of route on blood pressure or breathing rate; in the Shiplo 2016 survey of 364 Canadian medical cannabis patients, eating was rated lower in perceived respiratory harm than smoking. The other three are records of exposures, mostly in young children: Cao 2016 (430 exposures to cannabis food products reported to US poison centres, 2013 to 2015): tachycardia in 84 (printed as 31%, which 430 cannot give), chest pain or hypotension in a few, and respiratory depression in 3, reported only in children aged 5 or younger; Kaczor 2021 (chart review of 32 children): 5 (16%) needed respiratory support; Pepin 2023 (records of 80 children younger than 6 with a known THC dose): tachycardia and hypotension most common, with severe cardiovascular toxicity and severe respiratory symptoms (hypoxia, then apnea and bradypnea) at recorded doses above 2 mg/kg of body weight. The Abstract nonetheless says cannabis edibles were associated with minimal respiratory effects, and the Discussion that severe cardiovascular effects were associated with higher THC doses in all routes. No included study measured lung function or breathing symptoms in adults who eat cannabis against adults who do not use it.

tasks.locator: Abstract (Conclusion); Discussion, 1st paragraph; Discussion, paragraphs beginning Nevertheless, First, Second and Third; Strength and limitations; Conclusion; Disclosure statement; Funding
tasks.extracted: The review's conclusions and limits: the authors conclude that cannabis use does cause cardiovascular and respiratory effects but that conclusions by route remain tentative because of the studies' methodological limitations. They state that most studies were cross-sectional or retrospective, from which temporality cannot be determined; that the three longitudinal studies all concerned smoking and breathing; that the two randomised trials were small (n = 24 and, as they give it, n = 11); that only five of the 15 empirical studies reported cardiovascular effects; and that only three sources specified the type of smoking (joints against blunts); only English articles from 2009 to 2023 were included. In the Discussion they write that each route was associated with effects of some kind, suggesting a need to avoid cannabis altogether, followed by harm-reduction recommendations (the authors' advice, not derived from a synthesis and not adopted here). No funding; no conflicts of interest declared. Editors' reading: the causal wording is not supported by the designs the authors describe, nothing was pooled or appraised (AMSTAR 2 critically low on the card), and several studies within the review's window and topic that this library has read are not among its sources (Monte 2019 on emergency visits after eating against inhaling cannabis, Braymiller 2020 on vaping and bronchitic symptoms, Spindle 2018 on smoked against vaporised cannabis, Ghasemiesfe 2018, a systematic review of respiratory outcomes).
